Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Malaysian/Australian artist Tristan Jalleh submitted 𝙊𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙜 𝘽𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙖𝙣. The judging panel was drawn to the cinematic quality of the work and its striking reference to the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang), sensing an auspicious and deeply atmospheric presence within the piece. Through its layered digital landscape and mystical ambience, the artwork invites audiences into a journey through the unknown.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
As this could be used as a backdrop for promoting exhibitions based on Chinese mythology, I looked to symbolism in nature that unites various regional cultures, specifically the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang). It is often regarded as a natural shrine, an auspicious anchor connecting the past, present, and future, and also a home for spirits. Often a sprawling banyan tree is located at the entrance of villages as a welcoming symbol of protection and longevity. Here the banyan tree is shown at night, when it is said to have the closest connection to the supernatural, expressed as spectral lights and ghostly fog. The title of the work (Orang Bunian) is the Malay name for mythological forest spirits.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Malaysian/Australian Multimedia Artist and Music Video Director. Jalleh creates immersive and cinematic hybrid digital environments and frequently collaborates with performance artists and musicians, including Australian/Filipinix art collective Club Ate, to produce large scale multimedia artworks for galleries, art festivals, and live performance. Notable recent collaborations include artists Helen Grace & Phaptawan Suwannakudt for "Until We Meet Again" at the BACC (Bangkok Art and Culture Centre), Leyla Stevens for ‘PAHIT MANIS’ at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, Hoda Afshar for ‘The Fold’ at NGV Triennial and the Taipei Digital Art Festival 2024...
 
👀 Read more about Tristan's practice in the WRG Digital Archive. May be an image of text.","caption":{"text":"🎞️ ɪɴᴛʀᴏᴅᴜᴄɪɴɢ ᴡʀɢ ᴅɪɢɪᴛᴀʟ ᴄᴀʟʟ-ᴏᴜᴛ ꜱᴘᴇᴄɪᴀʟ ᴍᴇɴᴛɪᴏɴ ᴀʀᴛɪꜱᴛ: ᴏʟɪᴠᴇʀ ᴡʜɪᴛᴇʜᴏᴜꜱᴇ @oliver_wh_ 🎞️
 
Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Gadigal/Sydney-based artist Oliver Whitehouse submitted ‘Places I am going and places I have been.’ A second-time Special Mention artist, the judging panel were pleased to see Whitehouse’s evolving practice. They were impressed by the subtle integration of archival imagery gradually revealing itself throughout the work. Especially poignant is the inclusion of footage from the artists travels back home to China, which adds a sense of intimacy and personal resonance.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
‘Places I am going and places I have been’ takes viewers on an unknown journey across the landscapes of China that explores the mythologization of person, place, and history. Charting the urban sprawl of rural towns as well as the high-density architecture of cityscapes at night, overlaid across are illustrations and excerpts from an ancient volume of ‘Journey to the West’, which gradually transform into textbook diagrams, urban maps, and news articles. ‘Places I have been’ refers both to the videos captured during my travels back home to China as well as the objects, photographs, and stories that each express a remnant of the country’s cultural memory, printed and rephotographed. ‘Places I am going’ refers to an unknown and uncertain future, questioning the cost of a nations incessant desire for evolution...
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Oliver Whitehouse is a Chinese-British Director, Photographer, & Visual Artist based in Sydney (Gadigal). His work moves fluidly between mediums, drawing influence from experimental photography, internet phenomena, and the aesthetics of the eerie. With a visual language marked by a sense of the surreal, he navigates spaces where memory becomes disembodied, and the familiar becomes uncanny.

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Eora/Sydney-based artist Charles Marlow submitted 𝙈𝙚𝙢𝙤𝙧𝙮 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙛𝙚𝙧. The judging panel commended Charles's artwork for his engaging exploration of myths across time—from their celestial origins, through oral traditions, and into the realm of technology. Praise was given to the vibrant use of colour, the game-like pixelation that forms the creatures, and the expansive, intriguing digital world the artist has created.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
Myths have historically been born from the sky, the sea, the land, the mountains, stories told to help us understand and interact with the world around us. They have been told through oral traditions, written tales, films, and now, translated from our past into complex interactive networks of code and technology such as Black Myth: Wu-Kong. What does this do to our perception of mythology? Does the world existing on the other side of the screen, instead of embedded within our own, create a sense of separation from the tale? Are these stories still an expression of our human experience in our world? What does it mean for journeys such as Sun Wu Kong's to become our own through the use of intermediary technologies? With this work I hope to explore some of these questions. In the video we journey through a liminal space where mythology shifts between our physical world and the digital world, which is perhaps the space that is now where mythology lives in our minds.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Charles Marlow is a Sydney/Eora based designer interested in exploring digital technologies, their infrastructures, and the impact they have on how we understand the world. Working to communicate ideas through animation, web, code, and exhibition practices, he invites audiences into the conversation, and tries to get audiences to further consider their own relationships to technology.

Exploring the darker side of myth in the modern world, 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 draws inspiration from the viral video game Black Myth: Wukong (2024), a contemporary retelling of the legendary novel Journey to the West. Echoing its spiritual quest, the exhibition traces the concept of the journey in many forms—from physical travel to time travel, from internal odysseys to cosmic voyages. The artists in this exhibition, show us that sometimes, we must pass through the darkness to get to the light. 
 
𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 opens on 25 June 2026. See you soon... 
 
Image: Jiang Pengyi 蒋鹏奕, The Monument Bestowed by Desolation to Solitude - The Grandeur of Soaring Ascent, 2023, archival inkjet print, mounted on aluminium panel, 180 x 145 cm

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Malaysian/Australian artist Tristan Jalleh submitted 𝙊𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙜 𝘽𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙖𝙣. The judging panel was drawn to the cinematic quality of the work and its striking reference to the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang), sensing an auspicious and deeply atmospheric presence within the piece. Through its layered digital landscape and mystical ambience, the artwork invites audiences into a journey through the unknown.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
As this could be used as a backdrop for promoting exhibitions based on Chinese mythology, I looked to symbolism in nature that unites various regional cultures, specifically the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang). It is often regarded as a natural shrine, an auspicious anchor connecting the past, present, and future, and also a home for spirits. Often a sprawling banyan tree is located at the entrance of villages as a welcoming symbol of protection and longevity. Here the banyan tree is shown at night, when it is said to have the closest connection to the supernatural, expressed as spectral lights and ghostly fog. The title of the work (Orang Bunian) is the Malay name for mythological forest spirits.

Malaysian/Australian Multimedia Artist and Music Video Director. Jalleh creates immersive and cinematic hybrid digital environments and frequently collaborates with performance artists and musicians, including Australian/Filipinix art collective Club Ate, to produce large scale multimedia artworks for galleries, art festivals, and live performance. Notable recent collaborations include artists Helen Grace & Phaptawan Suwannakudt for "Until We Meet Again" at the BACC (Bangkok Art and Culture Centre), Leyla Stevens for ‘PAHIT MANIS’ at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, Hoda Afshar for ‘The Fold’ at NGV Triennial and the Taipei Digital Art Festival 2024...

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Gadigal/Sydney-based artist Oliver Whitehouse submitted ‘Places I am going and places I have been.’ A second-time Special Mention artist, the judging panel were pleased to see Whitehouse’s evolving practice. They were impressed by the subtle integration of archival imagery gradually revealing itself throughout the work. Especially poignant is the inclusion of footage from the artists travels back home to China, which adds a sense of intimacy and personal resonance.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
‘Places I am going and places I have been’ takes viewers on an unknown journey across the landscapes of China that explores the mythologization of person, place, and history. Charting the urban sprawl of rural towns as well as the high-density architecture of cityscapes at night, overlaid across are illustrations and excerpts from an ancient volume of ‘Journey to the West’, which gradually transform into textbook diagrams, urban maps, and news articles. ‘Places I have been’ refers both to the videos captured during my travels back home to China as well as the objects, photographs, and stories that each express a remnant of the country’s cultural memory, printed and rephotographed. ‘Places I am going’ refers to an unknown and uncertain future, questioning the cost of a nations incessant desire for evolution...
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Oliver Whitehouse is a Chinese-British Director, Photographer, & Visual Artist based in Sydney (Gadigal). His work moves fluidly between mediums, drawing influence from experimental photography, internet phenomena, and the aesthetics of the eerie. With a visual language marked by a sense of the surreal, he navigates spaces where memory becomes disembodied, and the familiar becomes uncanny.

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Eora/Sydney-based artist Charles Marlow submitted 𝙈𝙚𝙢𝙤𝙧𝙮 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙛𝙚𝙧. The judging panel commended Charles's artwork for his engaging exploration of myths across time—from their celestial origins, through oral traditions, and into the realm of technology. Praise was given to the vibrant use of colour, the game-like pixelation that forms the creatures, and the expansive, intriguing digital world the artist has created.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
Myths have historically been born from the sky, the sea, the land, the mountains, stories told to help us understand and interact with the world around us. They have been told through oral traditions, written tales, films, and now, translated from our past into complex interactive networks of code and technology such as Black Myth: Wu-Kong. What does this do to our perception of mythology? Does the world existing on the other side of the screen, instead of embedded within our own, create a sense of separation from the tale? Are these stories still an expression of our human experience in our world? What does it mean for journeys such as Sun Wu Kong's to become our own through the use of intermediary technologies? With this work I hope to explore some of these questions. In the video we journey through a liminal space where mythology shifts between our physical world and the digital world, which is perhaps the space that is now where mythology lives in our minds.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Charles Marlow is a Sydney/Eora based designer interested in exploring digital technologies, their infrastructures, and the impact they have on how we understand the world. Working to communicate ideas through animation, web, code, and exhibition practices, he invites audiences into the conversation, and tries to get audiences to further consider their own relationships to technology.

White Rabbit Gallery
whiterabbitgallery
 
10 w
Dr Judith Neilson AM opened the White Rabbit Gallery to share her collection of contemporary Chinese art with as many people as possible—especially those who may never have visited a museum or gallery before. Her aim was to show that contemporary art can be beautiful, challenging, and exciting, while giving visitors the freedom to experience it in their own way, without being told what they should or shouldn’t like.
 
Since 2009, the gallery has become an important part of the community.
 
"It's a living collection, it's got its own personality. It's got its name, and it lives here. It's part of the community. I know that sounds crazy, but that's sort of what it is." Dr Judith Neilson AM
 
Have you visited the gallery before? Do you have any favourite memories or artworks? Let us know in the comments below.
 
📸 Photography: James Brickwood / Sydney Morning Herald

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Malaysian/Australian artist Tristan Jalleh submitted 𝙊𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙜 𝘽𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙖𝙣. The judging panel was drawn to the cinematic quality of the work and its striking reference to the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang), sensing an auspicious and deeply atmospheric presence within the piece. Through its layered digital landscape and mystical ambience, the artwork invites audiences into a journey through the unknown.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
As this could be used as a backdrop for promoting exhibitions based on Chinese mythology, I looked to symbolism in nature that unites various regional cultures, specifically the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang). It is often regarded as a natural shrine, an auspicious anchor connecting the past, present, and future, and also a home for spirits. Often a sprawling banyan tree is located at the entrance of villages as a welcoming symbol of protection and longevity. Here the banyan tree is shown at night, when it is said to have the closest connection to the supernatural, expressed as spectral lights and ghostly fog. The title of the work (Orang Bunian) is the Malay name for mythological forest spirits.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Malaysian/Australian Multimedia Artist and Music Video Director. Jalleh creates immersive and cinematic hybrid digital environments and frequently collaborates with performance artists and musicians, including Australian/Filipinix art collective Club Ate, to produce large scale multimedia artworks for galleries, art festivals, and live performance. Notable recent collaborations include artists Helen Grace & Phaptawan Suwannakudt for "Until We Meet Again" at the BACC (Bangkok Art and Culture Centre), Leyla Stevens for ‘PAHIT MANIS’ at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, Hoda Afshar for ‘The Fold’ at NGV Triennial and the Taipei Digital Art Festival 2024...

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Gadigal/Sydney-based artist Oliver Whitehouse submitted ‘Places I am going and places I have been.’ A second-time Special Mention artist, the judging panel were pleased to see Whitehouse’s evolving practice. They were impressed by the subtle integration of archival imagery gradually revealing itself throughout the work. Especially poignant is the inclusion of footage from the artists travels back home to China, which adds a sense of intimacy and personal resonance.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
‘Places I am going and places I have been’ takes viewers on an unknown journey across the landscapes of China that explores the mythologization of person, place, and history. Charting the urban sprawl of rural towns as well as the high-density architecture of cityscapes at night, overlaid across are illustrations and excerpts from an ancient volume of ‘Journey to the West’, which gradually transform into textbook diagrams, urban maps, and news articles. ‘Places I have been’ refers both to the videos captured during my travels back home to China as well as the objects, photographs, and stories that each express a remnant of the country’s cultural memory, printed and rephotographed. ‘Places I am going’ refers to an unknown and uncertain future, questioning the cost of a nations incessant desire for evolution...
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Oliver Whitehouse is a Chinese-British Director, Photographer, & Visual Artist based in Sydney (Gadigal). His work moves fluidly between mediums, drawing influence from experimental photography, internet phenomena, and the aesthetics of the eerie. With a visual language marked by a sense of the surreal, he navigates spaces where memory becomes disembodied, and the familiar becomes uncanny. 
 
👀 Read more and view Oliver’s and work in the WRG Digital Archive. Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Eora/Sydney-based artist Charles Marlow submitted 𝙈𝙚𝙢𝙤𝙧𝙮 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙛𝙚𝙧. The judging panel commended Charles's artwork for his engaging exploration of myths across time—from their celestial origins, through oral traditions, and into the realm of technology. Praise was given to the vibrant use of colour, the game-like pixelation that forms the creatures, and the expansive, intriguing digital world the artist has created.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
Myths have historically been born from the sky, the sea, the land, the mountains, stories told to help us understand and interact with the world around us. They have been told through oral traditions, written tales, films, and now, translated from our past into complex interactive networks of code and technology such as Black Myth: Wu-Kong. What does this do to our perception of mythology? Does the world existing on the other side of the screen, instead of embedded within our own, create a sense of separation from the tale? Are these stories still an expression of our human experience in our world? What does it mean for journeys such as Sun Wu Kong's to become our own through the use of intermediary technologies? With this work I hope to explore some of these questions. In the video we journey through a liminal space where mythology shifts between our physical world and the digital world, which is perhaps the space that is now where mythology lives in our minds.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Charles Marlow is a Sydney/Eora based designer interested in exploring digital technologies, their infrastructures, and the impact they have on how we understand the world. Working to communicate ideas through animation, web, code, and exhibition practices, he invites audiences into the conversation, and tries to get audiences to further consider their own relationships to technology.
 
👀 Read more about Charles's practice and view his work in the WRG Digital Archive. Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Malaysian/Australian artist Tristan Jalleh submitted 𝙊𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙜 𝘽𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙖𝙣. The judging panel was drawn to the cinematic quality of the work and its striking reference to the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang), sensing an auspicious and deeply atmospheric presence within the piece. Through its layered digital landscape and mystical ambience, the artwork invites audiences into a journey through the unknown.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
As this could be used as a backdrop for promoting exhibitions based on Chinese mythology, I looked to symbolism in nature that unites various regional cultures, specifically the Banyan Tree (Nunuk Ragang). It is often regarded as a natural shrine, an auspicious anchor connecting the past, present, and future, and also a home for spirits. Often a sprawling banyan tree is located at the entrance of villages as a welcoming symbol of protection and longevity. Here the banyan tree is shown at night, when it is said to have the closest connection to the supernatural, expressed as spectral lights and ghostly fog. The title of the work (Orang Bunian) is the Malay name for mythological forest spirits.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Malaysian/Australian Multimedia Artist and Music Video Director. Jalleh creates immersive and cinematic hybrid digital environments and frequently collaborates with performance artists and musicians, including Australian/Filipinix art collective Club Ate, to produce large scale multimedia artworks for galleries, art festivals, and live performance. Notable recent collaborations include artists Helen Grace & Phaptawan Suwannakudt for "Until We Meet Again" at the BACC (Bangkok Art and Culture Centre), Leyla Stevens for ‘PAHIT MANIS’ at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, Hoda Afshar for ‘The Fold’ at NGV Triennial and the Taipei Digital Art Festival 2024...
 
👀 Read more about Tristan's practice in the WRG Digital Archive. Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Gadigal/Sydney-based artist Oliver Whitehouse submitted ‘Places I am going and places I have been.’ A second-time Special Mention artist, the judging panel were pleased to see Whitehouse’s evolving practice. They were impressed by the subtle integration of archival imagery gradually revealing itself throughout the work. Especially poignant is the inclusion of footage from the artists travels back home to China, which adds a sense of intimacy and personal resonance.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
‘Places I am going and places I have been’ takes viewers on an unknown journey across the landscapes of China that explores the mythologization of person, place, and history. Charting the urban sprawl of rural towns as well as the high-density architecture of cityscapes at night, overlaid across are illustrations and excerpts from an ancient volume of ‘Journey to the West’, which gradually transform into textbook diagrams, urban maps, and news articles. ‘Places I have been’ refers both to the videos captured during my travels back home to China as well as the objects, photographs, and stories that each express a remnant of the country’s cultural memory, printed and rephotographed. ‘Places I am going’ refers to an unknown and uncertain future, questioning the cost of a nations incessant desire for evolution...
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Oliver Whitehouse is a Chinese-British Director, Photographer, & Visual Artist based in Sydney (Gadigal). His work moves fluidly between mediums, drawing influence from experimental photography, internet phenomena, and the aesthetics of the eerie. With a visual language marked by a sense of the surreal, he navigates spaces where memory becomes disembodied, and the familiar becomes uncanny.

Responding to the theme 𝘽𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙠 𝙈𝙮𝙩𝙝 Eora/Sydney-based artist Charles Marlow submitted 𝙈𝙚𝙢𝙤𝙧𝙮 𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙛𝙚𝙧. The judging panel commended Charles's artwork for his engaging exploration of myths across time—from their celestial origins, through oral traditions, and into the realm of technology. Praise was given to the vibrant use of colour, the game-like pixelation that forms the creatures, and the expansive, intriguing digital world the artist has created.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠
Myths have historically been born from the sky, the sea, the land, the mountains, stories told to help us understand and interact with the world around us. They have been told through oral traditions, written tales, films, and now, translated from our past into complex interactive networks of code and technology such as Black Myth: Wu-Kong. What does this do to our perception of mythology? Does the world existing on the other side of the screen, instead of embedded within our own, create a sense of separation from the tale? Are these stories still an expression of our human experience in our world? What does it mean for journeys such as Sun Wu Kong's to become our own through the use of intermediary technologies? With this work I hope to explore some of these questions. In the video we journey through a liminal space where mythology shifts between our physical world and the digital world, which is perhaps the space that is now where mythology lives in our minds.
 
𝘼𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙨𝙩
Charles Marlow is a Sydney/Eora based designer interested in exploring digital technologies, their infrastructures, and the impact they have on how we understand the world. Working to communicate ideas through animation, web, code, and exhibition practices, he invites audiences into the conversation, and tries to get audiences to further consider their own relationships to technology.

SABBIA | UP NEXT

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of the 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Images: Jenni Kemarre Martiniello, Desert Grevillea Hu, 2026, hot blown glass with murrini, 380 h x 310 w x 220mm d

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours. 

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

BEN EDOLS & KATHY ELLIOTT
The Spaces Between
20 May - 13 June 2026

Sabbia is proud to present a new body of work by Ben Edols and Kathy Elliott, one of the most dynamic and enduring partnerships in contemporary Australian glass. Across three decades of collaboration, they have developed a shared visual language that unites Ben’s refined blown forms with Kathy’s expressive carved surfaces—each artist pushing the other into new understandings of material, technique and possibility.

Created between Canberra Glassworks, where Kathy undertook a focused residency, and the hot shop, where Ben produced the luminous forms that underpin their practice, this new series reflects the evolution of their long-standing creative dialogue. The Spaces Between highlights their commitment to experimentation, trust and the continual expansion of their collaborative vocabulary.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

Susie Choi is an artist working across ceramics, sculpture and installation on Gadigal and Wangal land. Born in Auburn to South Korean migrant parents, Choi’s latest body of work continues her exploration of materiality and perception. The interplay between hard and soft playfully dissects tensions around identity experienced by people of colour and children of migrants. The inflated life preserver form, an icon of the Australian Summer, has been rendered hard yet fragile and decorated with silk cord in the colours of children’s traditional Korean hanbok clothing. Spheres and cubes reference aspects of material culture the artist grew up with, such as Korean vessels and cabinetry, while also speaking to memories of childhood learning and play.

Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. I have wondered though how we decided upon what is the RS and WS of a stitch; despite having an intuitive sense of which way is “right”, I assume in some parallel universe it is reversed, you can decide which way you’ll do it or there is no such thing'. Susie Choi, 2026

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of the 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours.

SABBIA | UP NEXT

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours. 

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Image: Rrawa : Homeland exhibition at Sabbia

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of the 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Images: Jenni Kemarre Martiniello, Desert Grevillea Hu, 2026, hot blown glass with murrini, 380 h x 310 w x 220mm d

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours. 

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Image: Rrawa : Homeland exhibition at Sabbia

I am honoured to be a finalist in the inaugural Artbank Prize.
The prize has been established to recognise and support outstanding contemporary art practices, and to promote access for all Australian artists to present their work for consideration for the Artbank collection.

The finalists were selected via a competitive open-call submissions process that attracted over 740 entries. One finalist from every state and territory in Australia has been selected by the esteemed judging panel, Tony Albert, Ellie Buttrose and Elizabeth Fortescue.
An exhibition featuring the eight finalists will be held at Artbank's Sydney premises from 3 September until 30 October 2026, alongside a series of public programs that celebrate the finalists and their works.

The Artbank Prize is awarded to one artist, whose artwork will be acquired into the Artbank collection.

BEN EDOLS & KATHY ELLIOTT
The Spaces Between
20 May - 13 June 2026

Sabbia is proud to present a new body of work by Ben Edols and Kathy Elliott, one of the most dynamic and enduring partnerships in contemporary Australian glass. Across three decades of collaboration, they have developed a shared visual language that unites Ben’s refined blown forms with Kathy’s expressive carved surfaces—each artist pushing the other into new understandings of material, technique and possibility.

Created between Canberra Glassworks, where Kathy undertook a focused residency, and the hot shop, where Ben produced the luminous forms that underpin their practice, this new series reflects the evolution of their long-standing creative dialogue. The Spaces Between highlights their commitment to experimentation, trust and the continual expansion of their collaborative vocabulary.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

Susie Choi is an artist working across ceramics, sculpture and installation on Gadigal and Wangal land. Born in Auburn to South Korean migrant parents, Choi’s latest body of work continues her exploration of materiality and perception. The interplay between hard and soft playfully dissects tensions around identity experienced by people of colour and children of migrants. The inflated life preserver form, an icon of the Australian Summer, has been rendered hard yet fragile and decorated with silk cord in the colours of children’s traditional Korean hanbok clothing. Spheres and cubes reference aspects of material culture the artist grew up with, such as Korean vessels and cabinetry, while also speaking to memories of childhood learning and play.

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours.

SABBIA | UP NEXT

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Images: Jenni Kemarre Martiniello, Pattawilyangga Intertmezzo, 2026, hot blown glass with murrini, 350 h x 300 w x 250mm d.

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

The exhibition is installed ahead of the opening date of 24th June and can be viewed during normal gallery hours.

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

BEN EDOLS & KATHY ELLIOTT
The Spaces Between
20 May - 13 June 2026

Sabbia is proud to present a new body of work by Ben Edols and Kathy Elliott, one of the most dynamic and enduring partnerships in contemporary Australian glass. Across three decades of collaboration, they have developed a shared visual language that unites Ben’s refined blown forms with Kathy’s expressive carved surfaces—each artist pushing the other into new understandings of material, technique and possibility.

Created between Canberra Glassworks, where Kathy undertook a focused residency, and the hot shop, where Ben produced the luminous forms that underpin their practice, this new series reflects the evolution of their long-standing creative dialogue. The Spaces Between highlights their commitment to experimentation, trust and the continual expansion of their collaborative vocabulary.

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

Susie Choi is an artist working across ceramics, sculpture and installation on Gadigal and Wangal land. Born in Auburn to South Korean migrant parents, Choi’s latest body of work continues her exploration of materiality and perception. The interplay between hard and soft playfully dissects tensions around identity experienced by people of colour and children of migrants. The inflated life preserver form, an icon of the Australian Summer, has been rendered hard yet fragile and decorated with silk cord in the colours of children’s traditional Korean hanbok clothing. Spheres and cubes reference aspects of material culture the artist grew up with, such as Korean vessels and cabinetry, while also speaking to memories of childhood learning and play.

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. I have wondered though how we decided upon what is the RS and WS of a stitch; despite having an intuitive sense of which way is “right”, I assume in some parallel universe it is reversed, you can decide which way you’ll do it or there is no such thing'. Susie Choi, 2026

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. I have wondered though how we decided upon what is the RS and WS of a stitch; despite having an intuitive sense of which way is “right”, I assume in some parallel universe it is reversed, you can decide which way you’ll do it or there is no such thing'. Susie Choi, 2026

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026.

Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

Please contact the gallery for a preview digital sales catalogue for the exhibition via gallery@sabbiagallery.com

Images: 
-Paul Nabulumo Namarinjmak, Ngalyod - Raindow Serpent, 2025, stringybark with ochre pigment and pva fixative, 1490 h x 150 w x 150mm d
- Obed Namirrkki, Kunkurra - The Spiralling Wind, stringybark with ochre pigment and pva fixative, 2400 h x 400 w x 30mm d
- Jack Yurrulbbirri Nawilil, Ngalkodjek Spirit Pole, kurrajong with ochre pigment, pva fixative, bush wax and feathers, 1680 h x 90 w x 90mm d
- Lena Yarinkura, Yawkyawk, pandanus spiralis with ochre pigment and pva fixative, 1200 h x 820 w x 100mm d

JENNI KEMARRE MARTINIELLO OAM
Synesthesia
24 Jun - 18 Jul 2026

Presenting this incredible new body of work by glass artist Jenni Kemarre Martiniello OAM, a previous winner of the NATSIAA. Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Jenni Kemarre Martiniello is an Arrernte (Australian Central Desert), Chinese and Anglo-Celtic artist using glass as a medium to articulate ideologies of identity and culture memory. A previous winner of the NATSIAA, Jenni has been a finalist in several awards over her art practice career and has been included in major public collections across Australia and overseas. Most recently Jenni was the winner of the Blake Acquisitive Art Prize 2026. Martiniello re-imagines traditional indigenous weaving practices through Venetian glass cane-work techniques, twisting, pulling and tiling fine threads of glass that echo a woven tactile surface and continues this exploration of indigenous practices and culture, while simultaneously reinterpreting an ancient Chinese Han Dynasty vessel, the Hu. This intersection of Indigenous and Chinese cultural narratives reflects Martiniello’s innovative and evolving practice, offering a new dialogue on identity, heritage and material culture.

BEN EDOLS & KATHY ELLIOTT
The Spaces Between
20 May - 13 June 2026

Sabbia is proud to present a new body of work by Ben Edols and Kathy Elliott, one of the most dynamic and enduring partnerships in contemporary Australian glass. Across three decades of collaboration, they have developed a shared visual language that unites Ben’s refined blown forms with Kathy’s expressive carved surfaces—each artist pushing the other into new understandings of material, technique and possibility.

Created between Canberra Glassworks, where Kathy undertook a focused residency, and the hot shop, where Ben produced the luminous forms that underpin their practice, this new series reflects the evolution of their long-standing creative dialogue. The Spaces Between highlights their commitment to experimentation, trust and the continual expansion of their collaborative vocabulary.

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

Susie Choi is an artist working across ceramics, sculpture and installation on Gadigal and Wangal land. Born in Auburn to South Korean migrant parents, Choi’s latest body of work continues her exploration of materiality and perception. The interplay between hard and soft playfully dissects tensions around identity experienced by people of colour and children of migrants. The inflated life preserver form, an icon of the Australian Summer, has been rendered hard yet fragile and decorated with silk cord in the colours of children’s traditional Korean hanbok clothing. Spheres and cubes reference aspects of material culture the artist grew up with, such as Korean vessels and cabinetry, while also speaking to memories of childhood learning and play.

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. I have wondered though how we decided upon what is the RS and WS of a stitch; despite having an intuitive sense of which way is “right”, I assume in some parallel universe it is reversed, you can decide which way you’ll do it or there is no such thing'. Susie Choi, 2026

SUSIE CHOI
Right side wrong side
20 May - 13 June 2026

'This latest body of work presents a range of ideas, in flux, and at various stages. It comes out of my struggle to make sense of many things I care about and how this might make its way into the work. As a primary school kid, my aunt taught me how to knit, and in high school I learned how to sew, and I’ve kept both practices going. When you follow a knitting pattern, you keep track of the right side (RS) and the wrong side (WS) so that you get what you expect and the stitches on the outside of your garment look “right”. I have wondered though how we decided upon what is the RS and WS of a stitch; despite having an intuitive sense of which way is “right”, I assume in some parallel universe it is reversed, you can decide which way you’ll do it or there is no such thing'. Susie Choi, 2026

Rrawa : Homeland
A landmark exhibition from Maningrida
24 June - 18 July 2026

This exhibition brings together artists from Maningrida in north-west Arnhem Land, where stone country, rivers and floodplains shape everyday life. Here, Country is a living force, deeply connected to kinship and cultural knowledge.
Across generations, artists continue storytelling traditions—learning from Elders and renewing culture through their practice. Fibre works, bark paintings, lorrkkon (hollow logs) and mimih sculptures are made from materials gathered on Country, each carrying ancestral narratives and reflecting both tradition and individual expression. Rrawa: Homeland has been co-curated by Maningrida senior arts worker Ngarrich Derek Carter

Congratulations to Kaylene Whiskey whose major monograph 'The Art of Kaylene Whiskey', published by @ThamesAndHudsonAU and edited by @NatalieKing_Curator and @Iwantja_Arts, is the winner of the 2026 ABIA Illustrated Book of the Year.⁠
⁠
The awards are presented by @BooksAndPublishing, in partnership with the Australian Publishers Association.⁠
⁠
A special limited-edition run of 'The Art of Kaylene Whiskey' is available to purchase via our online store. These limited edition copies are presented in a clamshell box and accompanied by a signed and numbered lenticular print of 'Super Kaylene' (2025). ⁠
⁠
Purchase your copy of the limited edition 'The Art of Kaylene Whiskey' via the link in our bio.⁠
⁠
#KayleneWhiskey #RoslynOxley9

May be an image of lighting, light bulb, hallway and text.","caption":{"text":"FINAL DAY: Today is your last chance to view DIRTY OLD TOWN, an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery. ⁠
⁠
The exhibition includes a series of fourteen illuminated works drawn from the visual language of cheap hotel signage.⁠
⁠
"They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments," says Morton.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour."⁠
⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across recurring motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works extend the exhibition's interest in absence, instability and what lies at the edges of perception. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠⁠
To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠

In his current exhibition at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) returns to forms that suggest both presence and absence: thresholds that cannot be crossed, signs emptied of their meaning and openings that reveal as much as they conceal.⁠
⁠
Scattered high throughout the gallery, fourteen illuminated works take the forms of anonymous hotel signs – places without names, their language and purpose erased. Elsewhere, recurring motifs of doorways, fractured sunsets and apertures appear as symbols of negotiation, obstruction and passage.⁠
⁠
As Morton reflects, these are forms he continues to encounter throughout his practice: "a hole, a void, if you like... I can't escape them."⁠
⁠
'DIRTY OLD TOWN' continues at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery through to 20 June 2026.⁠

⁠
Included amongst the presentation is a selection of works from Tracey Moffatt's renowned 1986 series 'Some Lads', the body of work by which Moffatt announced herself as one of Australia's most inventive and compelling visual storytellers. ⁠
⁠
The photographs articulate what would become the distinctive characteristics of Moffatt's prolific practice: the coexistence of beauty, levity and wit with the incisive examination of race and its representation, deftly navigated through the overt use of artifice and performance. ⁠
⁠
Unlike the staged ethnographic photographs taken of First Nations people by colonial photographers in the 19th century, the history of which Moffatt has routinely referenced in her work, the men in 'Some lads' are not passive or artificially posed. Rather they proudly and playfully engage with the camera. ⁠
⁠
#TraceyMoffatt's 'Some Lads #2' and 'Some Lads #3' are on view at La Trobe Art Institute as part of 'My Blood Sings Old Songs' through to 9 August 2026. ⁠
⁠

May be an image of lighting, light bulb, hallway and text.","caption":{"text":"ON VIEW: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery is pleased to present 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton). ⁠
⁠
Exhibition dates: 22 May – 20 June 2026⁠
Request a catalogue: oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
"The fourteen light works scattered up high through the main gallery are copies of the forms of cheap hotel signs. They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments.⁠
⁠
"You need to cast your eyes upwards to see them, crane your neck a little. When we spend most of our time these days with downcast eyes staring at those little screens, this, at the very least, is an opportunity to exercise another muscle.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠
⁠

1 w
On view now at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) includes a series of fourteen light works drawn from the visual language of cheap hotel signage.⁠
⁠
"They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments," says Morton.⁠
⁠⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠"⁠
⁠
To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
Images: #CallumMorton, 'City Lights #2', 2026, steel, 2Pac polyurethane, lights, 33 x 67.5 x 12 cm.

74 likes, 2 comments - roslynoxley9 on June 13, 2026: "On view now at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) includes a series of fourteen light works drawn from the visual language of cheap hotel signage.⁠
⁠
"They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments," says Morton.⁠
⁠⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠"⁠
⁠
To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
Images: #CallumMorton, 'City Lights #2', 2026, steel, 2Pac polyurethane, lights, 33 x 67.5 x 12 cm.".

May be an image of lighting, light bulb, hallway and text.","caption":{"text":"FINAL DAY: Today is your last chance to view DIRTY OLD TOWN, an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery. ⁠
⁠
The exhibition includes a series of fourteen illuminated works drawn from the visual language of cheap hotel signage.⁠
⁠
"They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments," says Morton.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour."⁠
⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across recurring motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works extend the exhibition's interest in absence, instability and what lies at the edges of perception. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠⁠
To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠

In his current exhibition at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) returns to forms that suggest both presence and absence: thresholds that cannot be crossed, signs emptied of their meaning and openings that reveal as much as they conceal.⁠
⁠
Throughout the exhibition, recurring motifs of erased signs, obstructed doorways, apertures and architectural fragments point towards what remains inaccessible or unseen. For Morton, architecture becomes a tool through which to explore broader questions of visibility, privacy and the relationship between public and private space.⁠
⁠
'DIRTY OLD TOWN' continues at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery through to this Saturday, 20 June.⁠
⁠

Influenced by post-structuralism and relational aesthetics, ACW explores how reality is perceived through cultural models.⁠
⁠
ACW and Geoff Lowe have been represented by #RoslynOxley9 Gallery since 1983.⁠

In his current exhibition at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery, Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) returns to forms that suggest both presence and absence: thresholds that cannot be crossed, signs emptied of their meaning and openings that reveal as much as they conceal.⁠
⁠
Scattered high throughout the gallery, fourteen illuminated works take the forms of anonymous hotel signs – places without names, their language and purpose erased. Elsewhere, recurring motifs of doorways, fractured sunsets and apertures appear as symbols of negotiation, obstruction and passage.⁠

As Morton reflects, these are forms he continues to encounter throughout his practice: "a hole, a void, if you like... I can't escape them."⁠
⁠

⁠
Included amongst the presentation is a selection of works from Tracey Moffatt's renowned 1986 series 'Some Lads', the body of work by which Moffatt announced herself as one of Australia's most inventive and compelling visual storytellers. ⁠
⁠
The photographs articulate what would become the distinctive characteristics of Moffatt's prolific practice: the coexistence of beauty, levity and wit with the incisive examination of race and its representation, deftly navigated through the overt use of artifice and performance. ⁠
⁠
Unlike the staged ethnographic photographs taken of First Nations people by colonial photographers in the 19th century, the history of which Moffatt has routinely referenced in her work, the men in 'Some lads' are not passive or artificially posed. Rather they proudly and playfully engage with the camera. ⁠
⁠

⁠

Request a catalogue: oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠

"The fourteen light works scattered up high through the main gallery are copies of the forms of cheap hotel signs. They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments.⁠
⁠
"You need to cast your eyes upwards to see them, crane your neck a little. When we spend most of our time these days with downcast eyes staring at those little screens, this, at the very least, is an opportunity to exercise another muscle.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠
⁠
"This is an excess borrowed from the random combinations of the street and indeed I have imagined the gallery, this very particular room, to resemble a public square in a small town." – Callum Morton, 2026⁠
⁠

ON VIEW: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery is pleased to present 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton). ⁠
⁠⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across repeated motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works gesture towards what lies at the edges of things – hidden spaces, fleeting moments and states of precarity. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠
'DIRTY OLD TOWN' is on view at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery through to 20 June. 

To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
Image: Installation view, #CallumMorton, 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', #RoslynOxley9 Gallery, Sydney (22 May – 20 June 2026⁠). Photography: David Suyasa.

50 likes, 0 comments - roslynoxley9 on June 12, 2026: "ON VIEW: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery is pleased to present 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton). ⁠
⁠⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across repeated motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works gesture towards what lies at the edges of things – hidden spaces, fleeting moments and states of precarity. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠
'DIRTY OLD TOWN' is on view at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery through to 20 June. 

To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
Image: Installation view, #CallumMorton, 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', #RoslynOxley9 Gallery, Sydney (22 May – 20 June 2026⁠). Photography: David Suyasa.".

⁠
Included amongst the presentation is a selection of works from Tracey Moffatt's renowned 1986 series 'Some Lads', the body of work by which Moffatt announced herself as one of Australia's most inventive and compelling visual storytellers. ⁠
⁠
The photographs articulate what would become the distinctive characteristics of Moffatt's prolific practice: the coexistence of beauty, levity and wit with the incisive examination of race and its representation, deftly navigated through the overt use of artifice and performance. ⁠
⁠
Unlike the staged ethnographic photographs taken of First Nations people by colonial photographers in the 19th century, the history of which Moffatt has routinely referenced in her work, the men in 'Some lads' are not passive or artificially posed. Rather they proudly and playfully engage with the camera. ⁠
⁠

"The fourteen light works scattered up high through the main gallery are copies of the forms of cheap hotel signs. They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments.⁠
⁠
"You need to cast your eyes upwards to see them, crane your neck a little. When we spend most of our time these days with downcast eyes staring at those little screens, this, at the very least, is an opportunity to exercise another muscle.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠
⁠
"This is an excess borrowed from the random combinations of the street and indeed I have imagined the gallery, this very particular room, to resemble a public square in a small town." – Callum Morton, 2026⁠

VIEW: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery is pleased to present 'DIRTY OLD TOWN', an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton). ⁠
⁠⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across repeated motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works gesture towards what lies at the edges of things – hidden spaces, fleeting moments and states of precarity. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠

UPCOMING: Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery is pleased to present 'Pheno 03: Outside Broadcast, My voice keeps changing on me', the latest exhibition and series of performances by Paris-based collective @AConstructedWorld. ⁠
⁠
Opening reception: Saturday, 27 June, from 3–5pm⁠
Exhibition dates: 27 June – 18 July 2026⁠
Request a catalogue: oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠
⁠
Performances will take place during the opening reception from 3–5pm on Saturday, 27 June, followed by a finissage performance on Saturday, 18 July. ⁠
⁠
A Constructed World is the collaborative project, founded in 1993, of Geoff Lowe and Jacqueline Riva, based in Paris, France. ACW believe in the notion of collectivity. Their practice is concerned with the multiple narratives we use to construct and understand our world. They encourage the exchange of ideas and embrace the idea of chaos. Influenced by post-structuralism and relational aesthetics, ACW explores how reality is perceived through cultural models.⁠
⁠
ACW and Geoff Lowe have been represented by #RoslynOxley9 Gallery since 1983.⁠
⁠
Image: Still from #AConstructedWorld, 'Pheno Tv 03', 2026.

May be an image of lighting, light bulb, hallway and text.","caption":{"text":"FINAL DAY: Today is your last chance to view DIRTY OLD TOWN, an exhibition of new work by Callum Morton (@StudioCallumMorton) at Roslyn Oxley9 Gallery. ⁠
⁠
The exhibition includes a series of fourteen illuminated works drawn from the visual language of cheap hotel signage.⁠
⁠
"They are hotels without a specific name, at once generic and hardly noticeable. Hidden spaces for hidden moments," says Morton.⁠
⁠
"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour."⁠
⁠
In the small gallery, a gridded collection of pencil and gouache drawings unfolds across recurring motifs: water drops, liquid spills, holes, smoke-filled skies and comic smoke puffs.⁠
⁠
Intimate in scale, these works extend the exhibition's interest in absence, instability and what lies at the edges of perception. They form a quiet counterpoint to the illuminated hotel signs suspended throughout the main gallery.⁠
⁠⁠
To request a catalogue, email oxley9@roslynoxley9.com.au⁠

Included amongst the presentation is a selection of works from Tracey Moffatt's renowned 1986 series 'Some Lads', the body of work by which Moffatt announced herself as one of Australia's most inventive and compelling visual storytellers. ⁠
⁠
The photographs articulate what would become the distinctive characteristics of Moffatt's prolific practice: the coexistence of beauty, levity and wit with the incisive examination of race and its representation, deftly navigated through the overt use of artifice and performance. ⁠
⁠
Unlike the staged ethnographic photographs taken of First Nations people by colonial photographers in the 19th century, the history of which Moffatt has routinely referenced in her work, the men in 'Some lads' are not passive or artificially posed. Rather they proudly and playfully engage with the camera. ⁠
⁠

"These works resemble abandoned signs in as much as their use, their language, what they signify, has been removed and erased. But instead of being a rough copy with a gritty skeleton left behind, they are reimagined here with newly assembled and overly complicated structure, pattern and colour.⁠"⁠
⁠

Kenneth will be in the gallery tomorrow from 12pm. Please join us to celebrate the last day of his exhibition! 

Extended until 13 June, 2026
Kenneth Lambert 
‘Augmented Intervals’  
Open Thurs - Sat 11 ~ 5pm

‘Augmented Intervals’ extends Kenneth Lambert’s investigation into the interval as a condition of change. Grounded in material gathered from Bundanon, the works are shaped through processes of accumulation, displacement, and duration. Sand, pigment, and organic matter are applied and left to settle, allowing form to emerge through time rather than composition. The surface operates as a site where environmental forces and human gesture intersect, each leaving its trace. Suspended between sky and ocean, the works hold a state of flux, where matter remains unsettled and continuously reconfigured.   

***

 For all enquires please email us at: art@stanleystreetgallery.com.au  

Artist portrait by Samantha Bleuel 
Artwork images courtesy of the artist

Rachel Kent has served as CEO of Bundanon since 2021. Prior to Bundanon, she was Chief Curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, where she presented major projects with artists from the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the UK and South Africa.

In this conversation, Kenneth Lambert and Rachel Kent will discuss contemporary art, curatorial practice, material process, place, memory, video art and the shifting relationship between physical and digital.

Kenneth Lambert says:

“Rachel Kent has a rare capacity to hold complexity open. She brings depth, warmth and precision to a conversation, carrying her experience lightly. Her curatorial practice creates pathways for audiences to approach a work more closely while leaving its mystery intact.”

Join us this Saturday at 3pm.

Extended until 13 June, 2026!
Kenneth Lambert
 ‘Augmented Intervals’  

Open Thurs - Sat 11 ~ 5pm

‘Augmented Intervals’ extends Kenneth Lambert’s investigation into the interval as a condition of change. Grounded in material gathered from Bundanon, the works are shaped through processes of accumulation, displacement, and duration. Sand, pigment, and organic matter are applied and left to settle, allowing form to emerge through time rather than composition. The surface operates as a site where environmental forces and human gesture intersect, each leaving its trace. Suspended between sky and ocean, the works hold a state of flux, where matter remains unsettled and continuously reconfigured. 

  ***

 For all enquires please email us at: art@stanleystreetgallery.com.au  

@kenneth_lambert_artist 

 Image courtesy of the artist

Until 6 June

‘Augmented Intervals’ extends Kenneth Lambert’s investigation into the interval as a condition of change. Grounded in material gathered from Bundanon, the works are shaped through processes of accumulation, displacement, and duration. Sand, pigment, and organic matter are applied and left to settle, allowing form to emerge through time rather than composition. The surface operates as a site where environmental forces and human gesture intersect, each leaving its trace. Suspended between sky and ocean, the works hold a state of flux, where matter remains unsettled and continuously reconfigured.

May be an image of text.","caption":{"text":"Artist talk this Saturday at 3pm: Kenneth Lambert in conversation with Rachel Kent at Stanley Street Gallery.

Rachel Kent has served as CEO of Bundanon since 2021. Prior to Bundanon, she was Chief Curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, where she presented major projects with artists from the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the UK and South Africa.

In this conversation, Kenneth Lambert and Rachel Kent will discuss contemporary art, curatorial practice, material process, place, memory, video art and the shifting relationship between physical and digital.

Kenneth Lambert says:

“Rachel Kent has a rare capacity to hold complexity open. She brings depth, warmth and precision to a conversation, carrying her experience lightly. Her curatorial practice creates pathways for audiences to approach a work more closely while leaving its mystery intact.”

Join us this Saturday at 3pm.

Host your next event surrounded by art.

Hosting or planning an event, looking for somewhere different? Contact us at Stanley Street Gallery to discuss available dates. We can offer either a blank space for your corporate launches or the option to host a private function during one of our fabulous exhibitions.

If you are looking for a unique, elegant and centrally located venue, contact us to make a booking.

Limited dates are available throughout the year, including opportunities to host events alongside our exhibition program.

25 June - 18 July 2026

UNBECOMING

With a shared background in metalsmithing, Victoria Edin and Gretal Ferguson explore the intimate and domestic through their distinct yet complementary practices.

Gretal’s work is expertly hand-forged, evoking the tactile strength and precision of traditional metalcraft. Victoria, in contrast, reimagines domestic metalware, combining found objects with textiles to transform the familiar into something unexpected.

Thursday 25 June
5.30 ~ 7.30pm
RSVP via bio encouraged but not required

This is your opportunity to meet Victoria and Gretal as both artists will be here for the opening.

***

With a shared background in metalsmithing, Victoria Edin and Gretal Ferguson explore the intimate and domestic through their distinct yet complementary practices.

Gretal’s work is meticulously hand-forged, evoking the tactile strength and precision of traditional metalcraft. Victoria, in contrast, reimagines domestic metalware, combining found objects with textiles to transform the familiar into something unexpected.

Combining humour and handwork their work traces the porous boundaries between body, material, and the social expectations that shape our lives.

***
